newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek socialists face cliffhanger general election.
newsitem.headline: Greek socialists face cliffhanger general election.

text.p: Greece's ruling socialists face a tough challenge from their conservative opponents in their first battle without their founder Andreas Papandreou in Sunday's cliffhanger national election.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis, 60, who took over the party's helm from an ailing Papandreou in January, is pitted against conservative challenger Miltiades Evert, 57, in a contest pollsters say is too close to call.
Both the socialist PASOK and conservative New Democracy party leaders put on a brave face as they cast their votes along with millions of Greeks, both saying they were confident of election victory.
But poll analysts say this is the hardest Greek election to predict, with an unusually high number of undecided voters and a clear shift to smaller parties.

"If voters make their decision on the basis of what profits the country and its citizens, then we believe they will vote for PASOK," said Simitis after he cast his vote in the working-class district of Kaminia in the port of Piraeus.

He called the snap election confident that he was leading in opinion polls but has seen his support steadily eroded as he failed to inspire the public with a dull, academic and media-oriented campaign, a far cry from Papandreou's passionate oratory.
The conservative party campaigned vigorously and swiftly caught up in the polls, which show the socialists leading slightly and within the margin of error.

"Words from politicians are redundant. Today the Greek people speak and I believe tomorrow will be a new, great day for Greece," said Evert, who voted in a remote village near the Evros river, a natural border between Greece and Turkey.
Evert has made relations with Turkey the battlecry of his campaign and did not shy away from making populist pledges to woo voters.
But both leaders' lack of charisma and the absence of real policy differences between the two parties, particularly on the economy, have left the public indifferent to this election.
Pollsters said an unprecedented 20 percent of those asked one week before elections said they were undecided about how they would cast their ballot.
"It is too close to call. Everything about this election is new -- the leaders, the number of undecided voters, the general apathy," poll analyst Ilias Nikolakopoulos said on television.
The demure Simitis, a strongly pro-European technocrat, is nothing like his mentor, the flamboyant Papandreou, who died in June after a long illness.
The maverick socialist leader's crowd-rousing speeches, damning the big powers of the West and sticking up for the weak and underprivileged won him three landslide victories in 1981, 1985 and 1993.

His controversial blonde widow, Dimitra Liani, showed up dressed in black at her hometown of Elefsina, near Athens, to vote and to sum it up for reporters: "I vote on behalf of Andreas Papandreou, the great absent protagonist of these elections."
About 8.5 million Greeks are required to cast a mandatory vote at polling stations around the country, which opened at sunrise at 0413 GMT and will close at sunset at 1620 GMT.
The first exit poll results will be made public after official voting ends.
